passage:
Subject: Our Sunday meeting

Usha,

Thank you for sitting down with me on Sunday. Thirty minutes, tea, one notebook. I didn't expect to enjoy it. Let's keep it going: the first Sunday of every month. We go through what we spent, what is coming up, and anything either of us is unsure about. The point isn't to check on each other. It's so that a small worry gets said out loud in April instead of turning into a fight in July, and so that neither of us gets caught off guard by a large buy. Next time I'll make the tea, and you bring the notebook.

Nilesh

qa.q: On which day of the month will they hold the meeting?
qa.a: They will hold it on the first Sunday of every month.

qa.q: How does Nilesh feel about the first meeting?
qa.a: Nilesh feels pleasantly surprised, having expected not to enjoy it.

qa.q: What could Nilesh and Usha do if they disagree about a purchase in the meeting, and why?
qa.a: They could pause the decision until the next Sunday, because time to think keeps a small disagreement from turning into a fight.

qa.q: How might Usha feel on reading the email?
qa.a: Usha probably feels reassured and appreciated, since the email says the aim is to share worries early and not to check on each other.

grounding: Illustrates setting a monthly money meeting on the first Sunday so small problems are discussed early and neither partner is ambushed by a big purchase.

passage:
Bhavna, you asked how Rhea and I stopped having those big money fights. Honestly, it's thirty minutes and a pot of tea.
In our first year, we'd only talk about money when something went wrong. I'd see a big charge and get upset, or she'd find out I'd paid for my brother's trip without telling her. Every conversation felt like an ambush.
So we made a rule. The first Sunday of every month, after breakfast, we sit at the table with the expenses from the month. Thirty minutes, no longer. What we spent, anything coming up, anything worrying either of us.
Last month Rhea said she was thinking about a new laptop. Because it came up at the meeting, we planned for it together. No surprise charge, no fight.
It sounds boring, I know. I'm Siddharth, and I never thought I'd say this, but boring is great.

qa.q: When do Siddharth and Rhea hold their money meeting?
qa.a: The first Sunday of every month, after breakfast.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel about money conversations in the first year?
qa.a: Siddharth felt ambushed and upset, since money only came up when something had already gone wrong.

qa.q: What else could Siddharth and Rhea add to their monthly meeting?
qa.a: They could keep a short shared list of upcoming big purchases, so each meeting starts with what's ahead as well as what was spent.

qa.q: How does the monthly meeting look from Rhea's side?
qa.a: Rhea can raise plans like the new laptop calmly and plan together, rather than worrying about a fight later.

grounding: It shows a couple reviewing expenses for thirty minutes every first Sunday, so small problems come up early and neither feels ambushed by a big purchase.

passage:
I've shared a flat with my cousin Vandana and her husband, Mahesh, since last year, so I've watched their Sunday ritual from the sofa.
On the first Sunday of each month, around ten, Vandana puts the kettle on and Mahesh brings out a notebook. They sit at the dining table for about half an hour. I can hear bits: "electricity was high," "your mother's medicines," "should we still do Goa in December?"
They don't always agree. Once Mahesh mentioned a new bike and Vandana went quiet for a moment. But they talked it through there and then, and by the time the tea was finished, they'd agreed to wait until after Diwali.
What I notice is what doesn't happen. I've never heard them shout about a bill. I don't know what each of them privately thinks about money. But nobody seems surprised.
— Zeenat

qa.q: What time does the Sunday ritual usually start?
What might Vandana's moment of quiet suggest about how she felt when Mahesh mentioned the bike?
qa.a: It suggests she felt hesitant or uneasy about the cost, though they talked it through calmly and agreed to wait.

qa.q: What else could Vandana and Mahesh do if a big expense came up between meetings?
qa.a: They could agree to message each other before any purchase above a certain size, keeping the same no-surprises spirit.

qa.q: How does the ritual look to Zeenat?
qa.a: Zeenat sees a couple who never shout about bills, which suggests the meetings keep small problems from growing, though Zeenat can't know their private feelings.

grounding: It shows, through a flatmate's eyes, a couple reviewing expenses over tea every first Sunday so problems are raised early and big purchases are no surprise.
